history.q: From which country did Kenya gain independence in December 1963?
history.fact: Independence came on 12 December 1963, now celebrated every year as Jamhuri Day.

history.q: Who led Kenya to independence and became its first president?
history.fact: Kenyatta was prime minister at independence and served as president from 1964 until his death in 1978.

history.q: What name is given to the 1950s armed uprising against British colonial rule in Kenya?
history.fact: Its fighters called their movement the Kenya Land and Freedom Army; Britain declared a state of emergency in 1952.

history.q: Which Portuguese explorer stopped at Malindi in 1498 and found a pilot to guide him to India?
history.fact: A stone pillar he erected on the shore at Malindi still stands today.

history.q: Which European power built Fort Jesus in Mombasa in the 1590s?
history.fact: The fort was designed by Italian architect Giovanni Battista Cairati and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: What nickname was given to the nearly complete 1.5-million-year-old skeleton found near Lake Turkana in 1984?
history.fact: Spotted by fossil hunter Kamoya Kimeu, he is one of the most complete early human skeletons ever found.

history.q: Which family of fossil hunters made many celebrated discoveries of early humans in Kenya?
history.fact: Louis, Mary, their son Richard, Richard's wife Meave and daughter Louise all worked on human origins.

history.q: Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu grew rich as city-states of which Indian Ocean coastal culture?
history.fact: The Swahili language blends a Bantu grammar with many Arabic, Persian and later Portuguese and English words.

history.q: Nairobi was founded in 1899 as a depot on which railway?
history.fact: Its name comes from the Maasai phrase 'Enkare Nyrobi', meaning 'cool water'.

history.q: In 1898, two man-eating lions killed railway workers at which Kenyan river crossing?
history.fact: Engineer John Henry Patterson shot the lions; their skins and skulls are now displayed at the Field Museum in Chicago.

history.q: Kenya became a republic in which year, one year after independence?
history.fact: On 12 December 1964 the British monarch ceased to be head of state, and Jomo Kenyatta became president.

history.q: Until 1963, the narrow coastal strip of Kenya officially belonged to which ruler, though Britain administered it?
history.fact: The ten-mile-wide strip, including Mombasa, was transferred to Kenya at independence.

history.q: Which Mau Mau leader, captured in 1956, is honoured by a statue in central Nairobi?
history.fact: His bronze statue, unveiled in 2007, shows him holding a rifle on the street that bears his name.

history.q: Kenya's independence constitution was negotiated at conferences held in which London building?
history.fact: Conferences there in 1960, 1962 and 1963 paved the way for majority rule and independence.

history.q: Which chartered company administered British interests in Kenya from 1888 before the protectorate was declared?
history.fact: The company struggled financially, and Britain took direct control as the East Africa Protectorate in 1895.

history.q: When the East Africa Protectorate became a colony in 1920, what was it named after?
history.fact: Mount Kenya, at 5,199 metres, is Africa's second-highest mountain.

history.q: The 'airlift' that sent hundreds of Kenyan students to US universities from 1959 was organised chiefly by which politician?
history.fact: Future Nobel Peace laureate Wangari Maathai was among the students who went to study in the US.

history.q: Which city was the capital of the British East Africa Protectorate before Nairobi?
history.fact: As the colony's main port and the starting point of the railway, Mombasa was the natural first seat of government.

history.q: Jomo Kenyatta and five other nationalist leaders were tried in 1952-53 in which remote town?
history.fact: The 'Kapenguria Six' were convicted and imprisoned; the trial is now widely seen as politically motivated.

history.q: Thimlich Ohinga, a UNESCO site near Lake Victoria, is famous for what?
choices: Dry-stone walled enclosures built without mortar
history.fact: The enclosures, probably first built in the 16th century, sheltered communities and their livestock.

history.q: Which power captured Fort Jesus in 1698 after a siege lasting nearly three years?
history.fact: The fall of Fort Jesus ended Portuguese dominance on the coast north of Mozambique.

history.q: In the early 1400s, envoys from Malindi presented a giraffe to the court of which empire?
history.fact: Courtiers hailed the giraffe as a qilin, a mythical creature whose appearance was a sign of good fortune.

history.q: The ruins of Gedi, a Swahili town abandoned in the 1600s, lie near which coastal town?
history.fact: Gedi's coral-stone palace, mosques and houses are hidden in a coastal forest close to Watamu.

history.q: Critics nicknamed the costly Uganda Railway what?
history.fact: Built from 1896 to 1901 largely by labourers from British India, it ran from Mombasa to Lake Victoria.

history.q: Which Kenyan paleoanthropologist later headed the Kenya Wildlife Service and set fire to a huge stockpile of ivory in 1989?
history.fact: The televised ivory burn helped build global support for the international ban on the ivory trade.
